sections.overview: The common snipe is a skulking, long-billed wading bird of wet ground, so well camouflaged that it is usually seen only when it bursts into a zigzag flight. In spring the male produces a strange drumming sound in display flight.
sections.identification: An adult weighs about 108 g with a wing length near 14 cm, and a length of roughly 23–28 cm. The plumage is mottled brown above with pale buff stripes along the back, a streaked breast and pale underparts. The bill is long and straight, about 6 cm, and the legs are short. The sexes look alike.
sections.habitat: In the breeding season in Britain it is most frequent around lakes and also common in bogs and marshes, with the highest densities in Scotland, north-west England, Wales and western Ireland. In winter it uses a wide range of lowland and upland wet habitats. It nests on drier grassy ground close to its feeding areas.
sections.diet: It probes wet soil with its long bill for invertebrates. From April to August earthworms and insect larvae make up most of its food; in a Northumberland study, earthworms were about 61% of the diet by dry mass, followed by crane fly larvae at about 24%. Plant matter and seeds are eaten in smaller amounts.
sections.behavior: A skulking bird, it keeps to cover and flushes with a jinking flight. In display the male dives so that air passes through his outer tail feathers, making the drumming sound; females seem to prefer males that drum well. Males and females also take part in display fights.
sections.reproduction: In Britain the first clutch is laid on average around 30 April, typically four eggs, with one brood. The female incubates alone for 18–20 days. The downy chicks leave the nest and fledge after about 19–20 days, tended by both parents. Breeding typically starts at two years of age.
sections.ecology: As a predator of earthworms and larvae, the snipe is part of wet-grassland food webs, and it falls prey to red foxes, carrion crows and stoats. It is also hunted for food and sport, an estimated 1.5 million birds a year in Europe. In Britain, steep declines have been noted in lowland wet grassland. Unlike the smaller, shorter-billed Jack Snipe (Lymnocryptes minimus), it usually flies off in a conspicuous zigzag; see that profile for the reciprocal comparison.
sections.conservation: The IUCN lists the species as Least Concern worldwide, but numbers have declined across Europe since 1980. In the UK it is Amber-listed: about 67,000 breeding pairs in 2016, with a breeding range 31.5% smaller than in 1968–72. A snipe typically lives about three years once adult, and the oldest ringed bird exceeded 16.
